# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: *Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration*

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of the problems I raised there:

- It has a randomised control group.
- Output comes from administrative records rather than manager ratings.
- Hours come from timesheets.
- The analysis plan was registered.
- The results are stratified by type of work.
- Exploratory analysis is clearly labelled as such.

It also states the key distinction directly: output per hour and output per employee can move in opposite directions. Its finding that scheduled-hours estimates overstate the gain (22% versus 12.5%) is in effect a measured correction of the Halden method. The remaining issues are narrower, but some of them matter.

**The arithmetic checks out:**
- 0.979 / 0.87 gives +12.5% output per hour in case-processing.
- 0.979 / 0.80 gives +22%, the scheduled-hours figure.
- 0.886 / 0.83 gives +6.7% output per hour in counter offices.
- Timesheet hours: 33.0 / 37.9 is −12.9%, and 31.2 / 37.6 is −17.0%.

## 1. Inference with 10–14 clusters

Standard errors clustered by office are unreliable with this few clusters (7 v 7 and 5 v 5). They are typically too small, so the confidence intervals will be too narrow.

- The counter-stratum interval (−16.9 to −5.9), from only 10 offices, looks narrow for that reason.
- Use a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference, which suits a randomised design.
- State whether either was in the registered plan.

## 2. Several outcomes are not reported the registered way

The design promises difference-in-differences estimates for all registered secondary outcomes. Several results fall short of that.

- **Waiting time.** This is a registered secondary outcome, but it is reported only as a before-and-after change in treated offices (4.2 → 6.9 minutes). There is no control comparison and no confidence interval.
- **Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%). This is also before-and-after only and is not in Table 1. It is unclear whether it was registered.
- **Quality.** The figures (3.1% v 3.0% and 11.8% v 10.9%) are post-period levels with no confidence intervals and no difference-in-differences.
  - The rise in repeat contacts in the counter stratum is not discussed.
- **Sick days.** The −29% figure has no confidence interval and is pooled across strata, though the strata were analysed separately everywhere else.
- **Pooled primary estimate.** Was the registered primary analysis pooled or stratified? If it was pooled, report that estimate first.

## 3. The sick-day fall may be partly mechanical

Suppose the 30-hour week was worked as four days. Then each person has about 20% fewer scheduled days on which to be absent. Sick days per FTE would fall even if the risk of absence on any given day did not change.

- The paper says rotas were rearranged but does not describe how.
- Report sickness as absent hours divided by scheduled hours, or as an absence rate per scheduled day.
- The 29% figure may otherwise be mostly arithmetic. The same caution applies to the Halden figure of −36%.

## 4. Case-processing: is output being held up at a hidden cost?

Cases closed per FTE can stay level in ways that would not show up in this outcome:

- **Case mix.** Staff may be closing simpler cases first.
- **Backlog.** Older cases may be piling up.
- **Delay.** Time-to-decision may be rising.

The paper reports waiting time for counters but gives no service-time measure for case-processing. Yet backlog and deadline compliance are the obvious equivalent, and the data almost certainly exist in the case-management system.

The appeal-overturn rate is also a slow measure. Appeals take months, so decisions made late in the nine months may not have reached appeal yet.

## 5. Counter offices: the per-hour gain is mostly utilisation

In demand-driven queueing work, having fewer staff on duty mechanically cuts idle time, so handled contacts per staffed hour rise. The +6.7% is therefore better read as higher utilisation, paid for with longer queues, than as staff working more effectively.

The paper partly says this, but "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" invites the wrong reading.

There is also an accounting gap. Contacts handled fell 11.4%, but abandoned calls rose only 4 percentage points. The paper should explain where the remaining unserved demand went:
- channel-switching,
- deferred contacts,
- in-person visitors who left the queue.

Repeat contacts also count as handled contacts, so their rise slightly inflates the output measure.

## 6. Costs are missing

The intervention was full pay plus claimed overtime. Case-processing staff averaged about 3 hours of overtime a week above the 30 scheduled hours. Depending on overtime rates, cost per case may have risen even though output per FTE held. For counter offices, restoring service would need roughly 20% more staffed hours.

For an employer deciding whether to roll this out, cost per unit of output is the key number. A short cost section would make the paper considerably more useful.

## 7. Other measurement points

- **Unclaimed overtime.** Timesheets record overtime that was claimed. Unclaimed work, such as email out of hours, would make actual hours higher than recorded and the per-hour gain smaller.
- **FTE definition.** The paper uses "per FTE" and "per employee" interchangeably. If FTE is defined by contracted hours, a 30-hour post could count as 0.8 FTE, which changes what the ratio means. Define the term explicitly.
- **Confidence intervals for the per-hour estimates.** The counter interval (+0.4 to +13.3) is slightly narrower than simply dividing the output interval by 0.83 would give (+0.1 to +13.4). This can happen if hours and output co-vary across offices. A sentence on how these intervals were derived would help.

## 8. The exploratory meetings analysis

This section is handled responsibly: it is flagged as unregistered, the caveat about n = 7 is given, and a confirmatory test has been registered. Some additional points:

- **No pre-period.** Meeting time was measured only in month six. The 3.3-hour gap may partly reflect differences between offices that existed before the trial.
- **The correlation is very uncertain.** With seven offices, r = 0.71 has a 95% confidence interval running from about zero to 0.95. The office-level gains it correlates with are themselves noisy.
- **Implied mechanism.** It is worth stating directly that 3.3 fewer meeting hours is about two-thirds of the 4.9-hour fall in actual hours. If that holds, most of the reduction came out of meetings rather than productive time.
- **Placement.** Mentioning the result in the Summary is defensible, but say there that it is unregistered.

## 9. How far the counter result generalises

The counter result depends on how the change was implemented: opening hours were held fixed and staff were not added. "Coverage-bound work loses output" is a finding about that design. Alternatives were not tested, such as shifting rotas toward peak demand, partial backfill, or appointment systems.

The Discussion's closing point is well put: what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence. Spelling out the implementation dependence would tighten it further.

## 10. Smaller points

- **Discussion wording.** "Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses", but some of the counter evidence rests on unregistered or uncontrolled figures: abandoned calls and before-and-after waits.
- **Behaviour in the control group.** Control staff knew about the trial. Resentment or demoralisation could lower their output and inflate the estimated effects. If administrative data allow, compare control offices' trends with their own pre-trial trends.
- **Multiple comparisons.** There are two strata and several secondary outcomes, so say whether any adjustment was planned.

## Bottom line

The registered core is credible:
- In case-processing, output per FTE held at about −2%.
- Actual hours fell much less than scheduled hours.
- Coverage-bound offices lost service.

The weaker parts are:
- inference with few clusters,
- secondary outcomes reported outside the registered difference-in-differences framework,
- a sick-day measure that may be mechanical,
- no service-time or cost measures for case-processing.

If useful, I can draft a short comparison of the two papers' methods and conclusions.
